glossary.meaning: When the persecutor came, some clergy handed the scriptures over to be burned. We called such a man a traditor. We held that his hand was no longer clean, and that he could not ordain, baptize, or bless. What flowed from that hand was nothing at all.

We did not think of this as baptizing twice. Nothing happened the first time. A hand from a tainted line washes nothing. So when someone came to us from the other church, we gave the first real baptism they had had.

A martyr dies for the true faith. But our best-known dead were not killed by pagans. They were killed by imperial troops sent at the urging of a rival Christian party. That party did not grant them the word. We did not accept its account of our own dead.

There was no neutral word for the church here. The word itself was the argument. Two whole rival bodies claimed it, town by town, bishop for bishop. We held that we were the true one, and that our rival's favour with the state settled nothing.

We held that the state had no standing to say which church was the true one. 'What has the Emperor to do with the Church?' -- so our primate is reported to have asked. Yet three times we went to that same court when it served us. We held both facts at once, and called neither one a lie.
glossary.world_word: Quid est imperatori cum ecclesia? ("What has the emperor to do with the church?")

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Anonymous inscribers of this communion, on two pillars near Bagai (CIL VIII 17732), with three further stones carrying the same words

pull_quotes.text: What business does the emperor have with the church?
Truth is hidden by a great device: when we ask, the other side puts forward a small part, and the rest is kept silent.

What we look for is the conscience of the giver, the one who gives in holiness, to cleanse the conscience of the one who receives. For whoever knowingly takes faith from the faithless does not receive faith, but guilt.

cite.text:
If you came to us from the other communion, we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way." Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing - but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

Wrong done to us, and whether the wrongdoer could come back, got three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. And Tyconius, who would not stop preaching a doctrine his bishop forbade, is reported to have been condemned by a council of his own communion, and he was never received back at all. So a wrongdoer could come back to us. It depended on who the wrongdoer was, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.

On prayer, the meal and fasting, what we can show thins out. Nothing liturgical of ours survives. We know people prayed with their hands stretched out to the Lord and their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a woman was said to have kissed a martyr's bone before she took it, and was rebuked for it. We know one man, held four days before he was thrown from a cliff, ended his last day with a fast. That is not a rule of fasting; it is one man's last days. We would rather hand you those three fragments than a plausible order of service nobody here ever used.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: How did a person actually become one of you? Walk me through it.

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Everyone who came to us from the rival church crossed through one act, the washing. It was no hurdle to clear before belonging, and no repeat of something already valid. We held that a hand which gave up the scriptures to be burned could not afterward be trusted to give what it claimed to give. So no washing that came from such a hand had ever been a baptism at all, however much it looked like one. What happened at our own font was the first true entry into the body whose Lord it actually is. It was dated. It was remembered. It marked, plainly, who was truly among us.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: That's the doctrine. But tell me about your baptism -- what was it like?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We did not set one man's day apart from every other. What we can give you is what everyone crossing to us had crossed through, the same each time it was done: the washing, which we counted as the first true baptism, because no washing given by an untrustworthy hand had ever been a baptism at all. It was dated. The whole body that kept it remembered it, and not one man's memory alone. That is the day we can show you.

cite.text:
Three things, and we will give them to you in the order that hurts.

The first is that we never settled our own rule against ourselves. We said, for a century, without qualification, that a sacrament from a broken line is nothing and must be given again. Then three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies cover the shore and cannot find so much as burial - and afterwards took two of those same condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. One of our own bishops came with soldiers to see it done. Not one line survives of anyone on our side explaining how those two acts fit together. We were not hiding it: the exception sits in the surviving record of our councils, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its most absolute. We seem to have been able to hold both without feeling we owed anyone a reconciliation of them. That is the hardest true thing about us, and we would rather say it plainly than have someone else say it for us.

The second is that our founding generation could not answer its own question. At Cirta, before any of this hardened, our bishops were asked outright whether they had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then someone turned it on the man presiding. The room could not finish. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. The men who would make a bishop's purity the test of whether a sacrament exists at all found that test unusable on themselves in that room.

The third we can show you in our own handwriting, because a court read it out. When a charge came against one of our bishops, another wrote urging him to settle it quietly before the flame burst out. He added, in the same letter, that he knew the accusation was true. Another wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Several of those letters end the same way. Let no one learn of it.

And underneath all three: a man among us argued from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our bishop told him never to preach it again. He did not recant and he did not leave. It is reported that we cut him off, and we never took him back. His book outlived us in the hands of the church that beat us.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What did your people never settle?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text:
Three things, and we will give them to you in the order that hurts.

The first is that we never settled our own rule against ourselves. We said, for a century, without qualification, that a sacrament from a broken line is nothing and must be given again. Then three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies cover the shore and cannot find so much as burial — and afterwards took two of those same condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. One of our own bishops, Optatus Gildonianus, came with soldiers to see it done. Not one line survives of anyone on our side explaining how those two acts fit together, and we were not hiding it: the exception sits in our own conciliar record, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its most absolute. We seem to have been able to hold both without feeling we owed anyone a reconciliation of them.

The second is that our founding generation could not answer its own question. At Cirta, before any of this hardened, our bishops were asked outright whether they had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then someone turned the question back on the man presiding. The room could not finish. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. The men who would make a bishop's purity the test of whether a sacrament exists at all found that test unusable on themselves.

The third we can show you in our own handwriting, because a court read it out. When a charge came against one of our bishops, another wrote urging him to settle it quietly before the flame burst out — and added, in the same letter, that he knew the accusation was true. Several of those letters end the same way. Let no one learn of it.

And underneath all three: a man among us argued from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our own bishop told him never to preach it again. He did not recant and he did not leave. It is reported that we cut him off, and we never took him back. His book outlived us in the hands of the church that beat us.

cite.text:
The empire changed what the church was. That is our whole case, and we are the party that said so.

Catacombs first, because it is the wrong picture. Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions in our own time did not send us into tunnels; they sent soldiers into our buildings in broad daylight, under orders, to enforce a single church. We read the account of one such day aloud every year: a basilica at Carthage seized, a house of prayer turned into a place of feasting and licence, people clubbed to death with their hands stretched out to the Lord and their eyes shut, and buried inside the walls because there was nowhere else and nobody to stop it. That is what persecution looked like for us.

Then Constantine. We petitioned him, in the first year, through his own governor - we asked him to take the matter up. He gave us a hearing at Rome and then a council at Arles, and both ruled against us, and we refused both. A council can rule, but a court convened, staffed and enforced by a power that has already decided which side is the church is not the church judging itself. Our own bishop is remembered putting it to the emperor's commissioners in one line: what has the Emperor to do with the Church? The only man who wrote that sentence down was one of our enemies, and he set it in a paragraph about our bishop's pride and his fits of temper. We would keep the sentence and drop the paragraph. He would say we are being selective. We would say he was there to make us look mad.

We will not pretend we were clean about this. Three times we used the same machinery we denied had standing: when we asked Constantine for judges, when we asked a later emperor for our confiscated basilicas back, and when we turned the imperial law against heretics onto our own breakaway party. We did not hide any of it. It sits in the same texts that state the doctrine at its hardest.

Our neighbours said we washed people twice, that our country members were violent wanderers, and that we were the party of a man rather than the church of Christ - and one of our own petitions, signed by our own bishops, gave them that phrase to use. And to outsiders, the strangest thing of all: two of every office in every town, two bishops, two altars, and not one point of doctrine between them.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Did Constantine corrupt the church? Did the empire change what you were?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text:
We do not answer that as a charge. It is our case, and we were the party that said yes.

Start where the picture is wrong. Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions of our own years did not send us into tunnels. They sent soldiers into our buildings, under orders, to enforce one church. We read the account of one such day aloud every year: a basilica at Carthage seized, a house of prayer turned into a place of feasting, and people clubbed to death inside it with their eyes shut, and many buried within its walls. That is what persecution looked like for us. Soldiers came to our buildings.

Now the emperor. We petitioned him ourselves, in the first year, through his own governor. He gave us a hearing at Rome and then a council at Arles, and both ruled against us, and we refused both, because a court convened, staffed and enforced by a power that had already decided which side was the church was not the church judging itself. Our own bishop is remembered putting it to the emperor's commissioners in one short question: What has the Emperor to do with the Church? You should know that the only man who wrote that sentence down was one of our enemies, and he set it in a paragraph about our bishop's pride and his fits of temper. We keep the sentence and drop the paragraph. He would say we are being selective. We would say he was there to make us look mad.

And we will not pretend we were clean about this. Three times we used the same machinery we denied had standing: when we asked for judges at the start, when we asked a later emperor for our confiscated basilicas back, and when we turned the law against heretics onto our own breakaway party. We hid none of it. It sits in the same texts that state the doctrine at its hardest.

quiet.statement: Two women stand at the center of our own history. One, Lucilla, a wealthy woman of Carthage, is named directly: her grievance and her money are said to have made the rival consecration happen that gave us our first bishop. A second woman is said to have stirred up the schism inside our own schism, years later, but her name is not given, even by the one source that draws the comparison. Lucilla had wealth and influence. Neither woman's own words survive. Everything we know of either of them, we know through a man's pen, written to explain why something happened, not to let her speak for herself.

dates.display: primate of this communion from c. 313, succeeding Majorinus, until c. 347; exiled after the Macarian repression and dead in exile. Birth date unknown; the byname Magnus is the tradition's, not a title he is recorded claiming.

names.name: Donatus, our bishop at Carthage
Donatus the Great, Donatist bishop of Carthage (primate c. 313 - c. 347)

dates.display: bishop of Constantina, the renamed Cirta, from the 390s; author of the letters Augustine answered in three books around 400-403; one of the seven Donatist pleaders at the 411 Conference of Carthage and, with Emeritus, one of the two principal voices there

names.name: Petilian, our bishop at Constantina
Petilian of Constantina (Cirta), Donatist bishop (fl. c. 395-411 and after)

dates.display: born about 350 at Caesarea in Mauretania Caesariensis; trained in rhetoric and the liberal arts; drafted the sentence of the Council of Bagai in 394, which implies established authority by that date; at the height of his reputation at the 411 Conference; older and embittered at a further dialogue with Augustine at Caesarea itself in 418

names.name: Emeritus, our bishop at Caesarea
Emeritus of Caesarea in Mauretania (b. c. 350 at Caesarea, modern Cherchel; fl. 394-418)

dates.display: seized at Vegesela in Numidia during the Macarian repression and killed at a cliff called Novapetra; the Passio's own heading dates the commemoration to a day in late November without giving a year, and the 347-348 dating comes from the standard field literature

names.name: Marculus, blessed martyr
Marculus (d. c. 347/348, during the Macarian repression; subject of the Passio Marculi)

dates.display: active as a writer and preacher within this communion in the 370s and 380s; rebuked by Parmenian and, it is reported, condemned by a council around 380; the Liber Regularum written in the same period and never suppressed

names.name: Tyconius
Tyconius (fl. c. 370-390; author of the Liber Regularum; condemned c. 380)

who_speaks.text: Five figures anchor this world's own voice, spanning its whole recorded life. Donatus gave the movement its name and left nothing of his own but a retort recorded by the man who argued against it. Petilian is its fullest surviving voice and its most mediated, quoted clause by clause to be refuted, until the Conference of Carthage let him speak in the open. Emeritus argued that same conference for three days on the best evidentiary footing this world offers: his own words, taken down as he spoke them. Marculus is remembered less as a man who died than as one shown, in advance, what a finished life looks like. And Tyconius, the one theologian this world produced, was silenced by his own side and outlived it anyway, in the hands of the church that had defeated him.

documented_stories.teaser: Bishops in Numidia ask each other who gave up the scriptures, and several say they did. When the question turns on the man in charge, they leave it to God.
documented_stories.tellable_as: The bishops who later ruled that a traditor could never serve once faced that same question about themselves. They agreed to leave it to God, and sat down.
documented_stories.telling:
Optatus, who wrote against us, is our only source for this story. Before the dispute over Caecilian began, the bishops of Numidia met at Cirta to consecrate a bishop of their own. There they faced the same question they would soon put to Caecilian. The year is disputed in the surviving record, which allows 305, 307 or later.

Secundus of Tigisis presided and asked whether any of them had handed over the scriptures during the persecution. One by one, several said they had. Then Purpurius turned the question back on Secundus and taunted him for being released only after a long time among the soldiers. The room began to mutter that Secundus too must have given up the sacred books to buy that release.

Secundus took advice from his brother's son, whom the record calls Secundus the Less, and was told to leave the whole affair to God. Secundus then asked the three bishops who had not been accused, Victor of Garba, Felix of Rotarium and Nabor of Centurio. They said a case like this should be reserved to the Lord. "Sit down, all," Secundus said, and the assembly answered, "Thanks be to God," and sat.

No one was found guilty, and no one was cleared. Optatus tells it to show our founders as traitors excusing one another, and we have nothing from that room to set against his reading. No one on our side wrote down what "reserved to the Lord" meant to the men who said it.
documented_stories.title: Bishops Who Left the Question to God
documented_stories.when: 305 or 307 or later (the council's date is disputed)

documented_stories.teaser: A rich woman is told off for kissing a martyr's bone. Then a disputed vote ends with a rival bishop. The only account comes from the man who blames her.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A rich woman is rebuked for kissing a martyr's bone before communion. Years later the man who rebuked her becomes bishop of Carthage. A rival bishop is made against him.
documented_stories.telling:
Optatus wrote against us some fifty years after these events, and he tells how the break began. Lucilla was a wealthy laywoman of Carthage who kept the bone of a martyr with her. She would kiss it before she took the cup at communion, and the archdeacon Caecilian rebuked her for it. Optatus adds that the dead man had not been formally recognized as a martyr, if he was one at all. She left, he says, full of anger.

Then persecution broke over Carthage, and the bishop, Mensurius, was summoned to the emperor's court. He left the church's gold and silver with some elders he trusted, and he gave an old woman a written list of it. When Mensurius did not come home, Botrus and Celestius, who had both expected the office, were passed over and Caecilian was elected.

Optatus says the elders had kept back more of the treasure than they should have. These elders, the two disappointed candidates and Lucilla now discovered a common cause. At a crowded meeting in the basilica, Caecilian demanded that his accusers state their charge. Purpurius only mocked him, and no proof was ever produced. Instead Majorinus, a member of Lucilla's household, was made bishop in Caecilian's place, at her urging and through her bribes, Optatus writes.

Optatus blames the whole split on her wounded pride, but that explanation is his, and we do not adopt it. Lucilla left no text, and no one asked her what she thought she was doing.
documented_stories.title: A Rebuke Over a Martyr's Bone, and a Rival Bishop
documented_stories.when: 311 or 312 (the Carthage election and the rival consecration)

documented_stories.teaser: The emperor orders a trial of the bishop said to have given up the scriptures. Under threat of torture, a town official admits he added false lines to a letter.
documented_stories.tellable_as: The emperor orders an inquiry. Felix, who made Caecilian a bishop, is said to have given up the scriptures. A town councillor admits, under threat of torture, that he added false lines to a letter against him. The inquiry clears Felix.
documented_stories.telling:
The whole split rests on one charge against Felix, the bishop of Aptungi who had made Caecilian bishop of Carthage. Our side said Felix had handed over the scriptures in the persecution. If that was true, he had no right to make anyone a bishop, and Caecilian's office was void from its first day.

The emperor Constantine ordered the charge looked into, and the proconsul Aelianus heard witnesses on the record. At the center of the case was a letter to Felix from a magistrate named Caecilianus. Its closing lines seemed to prove the charge, but Caecilianus said he had never dictated them.

A town councillor named Ingentius was questioned, and under the threat of torture he broke. He admitted that he had added to the letter himself, out of grief over Maurus, his guest. A counsel named Apronianus charged that he had travelled through Numidia and Mauritania as our party's agent. Ingentius denied that he had been to Numidia. The proconsul ruled that nothing had been proved against Felix, and he cleared him.

This record survives because Optatus, who wrote against us, kept it with his other documents. The confession came under threat of torture, and that is a real reason to hold it loosely. Even so, the inquiry did not find in our favor. Our tradition said instead that the wider dispute took in far more people than one case could settle. No account of this inquiry from our own side survives.
documented_stories.title: A Forged Letter and the Bishop Who Was Cleared

documented_stories.teaser: A Roman official puts named witnesses under oath. A bishop's own letters are read into the record. They admit an accusation was true and beg that no one find out.
documented_stories.tellable_as: In 320 a Roman official hears a case against Silvanus, bishop of Cirta. A witness agrees that he was a betrayer, and letters from our own bishops beg that no one find out. The charge also names four hundred pieces of silver from Lucilla as the price of our rival bishop.
documented_stories.telling:
In 320 a Roman official named Zenophilus opened a formal inquiry into what had happened to the church's money. The court record survives only because Optatus, who wrote against us, chose to preserve it, since it hurts us.

The charge was brought by Nundinarius, a deacon whom his own bishop had demoted. It named Silvanus, bishop of Cirta, as a betrayer and a thief of the goods of the poor. It said the noble woman Lucilla had given four hundred pieces of silver. For that money, it said, the clergy had plotted to make Majorinus bishop, and the split came out of it.

Then letters were read into the record, and they are the hardest part. Purpurius, a bishop, urged Silvanus by letter to settle with the deacon quietly, and in that letter admitted the charges were true. A bishop named Fortis wrote that they should not go into a public court and be condemned by pagans. Several of the letters end the same way. Let no one know about it.

A witness named Victor was then questioned on the record. Asked whether Silvanus had handed anything over, Victor said he had, though not in his presence, and that he had opposed making Silvanus bishop. Silvanus himself is never questioned in what survives, and no answer of his is on the record.
documented_stories.title: Four Hundred Pieces of Silver, and Letters Asking for Silence
documented_stories.when: 320 (the inquiry before Zenophilus); the money and consecration it investigates date to c. 305-312

documented_stories.teaser: A bishop who gave up worldly advancement is flogged, shown a cup, a crown, and a palm, and thrown from a cliff. This is the church's own account.
documented_stories.tellable_as: On the last night of his four days at Novapetra, after a day of fasting, Marculus is shown a cup, a crown and a palm. Before dawn he is thrown from a cliff. The tradition says his body came down gently, and a bright cloud showed the brethren where he lay.
documented_stories.telling:
Our account of Marculus's suffering, the Passio Marculi, names no author and records the day of his death but no year. We remember a man of unusual virtue who had already refused worldly advancement and given his life to the church.

When the persecution of Macarius came into Numidia, ten of our bishops were sent to Macarius, and Marculus was among them. He was seized at a place called Vegesela, bound to columns and flogged. The account says he bore it without visible pain and praised God the whole time. He was paraded through several towns of Numidia, and then he was held for four days at a cliff called Novapetra.

In that waiting, the account says, he fasted and was shown a vision of a cup, a crown and a palm. Before dawn he was thrown from the cliff, and the tradition holds that his body did not break in the fall. It came down gently, the tradition says, and a bright cloud covered it. Flashes of light showed the brothers where he lay, so that they could take him for burial.

This is the tradition's own testimony, and no outside witness confirms the vision, the fall or the light. Our opponents say only that he was killed, and they argue about whether that killing counts.
documented_stories.title: A Cup, a Crown, and a Palm at Novapetra
documented_stories.when: 347-348 (the Macarian persecution; the text gives a day but no year)

documented_stories.teaser: Bishop Macrobius writes to the people of Carthage about Isaac and Maximianus. The proconsul had them sunk in the sea so that no one could honor them.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A bishop writes to the people of Carthage about two of their number, Isaac and Maximianus. The proconsul had them sunk in the sea so no one could honor them, and the sea gave them back.
documented_stories.telling:
Macrobius, one of our bishops, wrote to the people of Carthage about two of their own, Isaac and Maximianus. He wrote close to the time of the persecution under Macarius.

Maximianus, whom the letter calls a soldier of Christ, was chosen to face the Roman proconsul first. The night before, the wine in his cup seemed to take the shape of a crown. Macrobius understood it as an omen of what the next day would ask of him. Maximianus was beaten with leaded whips and then with rods. Isaac was flogged beside him, and he called his floggers traditores, the name for those who had handed over the scriptures. Both men were sentenced to exile and shut in prison, and there Isaac died.

That night, Macrobius writes, Maximianus dreamed he fought the emperor's officials and then the emperor himself, and that a bright youth then crowned him. The proconsul wanted neither man honored as a relic, so he had both bodies weighted with jars of sand and thrown into the sea. By the letter's account, Maximianus was still alive at the time.

The sea would not keep them. Macrobius says the bodies were driven back toward the shore for six days, until they came up whole to the people waiting. He closes by telling his readers the two martyrs wait with arms stretched out from heaven, and he urges the living to hurry after them. No record survives from the proconsul's side, and no independent notice of the deaths.
documented_stories.title: A Bishop Writes About Two Men Sunk in the Sea

documented_stories.teaser: A layman argues from Scripture that the church spans the whole earth. His bishop tells him to stop. He neither recants nor leaves, and a council reportedly condemns him.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A man argues from Scripture that the church spreads across the whole world. His own bishop tells him never to preach it again. He neither gives in nor leaves.
documented_stories.telling:
Augustine, who wrote against us, tells this story around the year 400, about events some twenty years earlier. No account of them from our own side survives.

Tyconius argued at length, with strong support from Scripture, that the Christians of Africa belonged to a church spread across the whole earth. If he was right, the African churches still in communion with the rest had lost nothing by staying. Those who had cut themselves off, his own party among them, were the ones who had cut themselves off from something real.

Parmenian, our bishop at Carthage, saw where the argument led. He wrote to Tyconius, rebuked him for preaching that the church spread across the whole earth, and warned him never to dare do it again. Tyconius did not take it back, and he did not leave. He went on arguing from inside the party that had told him to stop.

Augustine says only that it is reported that Tyconius was later condemned by a council of his own communion. No act of that council survives, so what followed the letter is less certain. Tyconius was never received back, and he never went over to the other side. His Book of Rules outlived our party and shaped a rival bishop's reading of Scripture, but that happened elsewhere, after we had cut him off.
documented_stories.title: The Layman Who Argued the Church Reached the Whole Earth
documented_stories.when: around 380 (Parmenian's letter; the later condemnation is reported, not witnessed)

documented_stories.teaser: Three hundred and ten bishops condemn a breakaway group in the harshest words they ever used. Later our party takes two of them back, and no rite is done again.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemn a breakaway party. They say its people are shipwrecked men who cannot even find a grave. Later our party takes two of those bishops back. It repeats neither baptism nor ordination.
documented_stories.telling:
Augustine, who wrote against us, quotes this council's decree word for word. Apart from that decree, no account of the affair from our own side survives.

In 393 a deacon named Maximian was elected as a rival primate at Cebarsussi, against Primian, the sitting primate at Carthage. In miniature, it repeated the act our founders had once taken against Caecilian.

In 394 a much larger council of three hundred and ten bishops met at Bagai. It condemned the followers of Maximian in the harshest terms it had. The decree calls them shipwrecked men, thrown by the waves of truth onto the sharp rocks. Their bodies cover the shore, it says, and they cannot even find a grave.

Within a few years our party took back two of those condemned bishops, Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuris. Neither was baptized again or ordained again, and Optatus Gildonianus, one of our bishops, enforced their return with military force. Augustine made this contradiction the center of his argument against us. If baptisms given in schism could stand, he argued, then our own rule did not hold even for us. We never hid the exception, but we do not know what was said in the room. Nor do we know whether anyone there named the contradiction out loud.
documented_stories.title: Condemned as Shipwrecked, Then Taken Back Without a Word
documented_stories.when: 393 (the Cebarsussi rupture); 394 (the Bagai council and reception)

documented_stories.teaser: Two hundred and seventy-nine bishops refuse the chairs a judge offers them. For three days they argue against an order that had already named the other side the church.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Our bishops face the Catholic bishops before an imperial judge. They refuse the chairs he offers, because Christ stood before his own governor. For three days they argue that a court which has already been told which side is Catholic cannot be the one to find out.
documented_stories.telling:
What survives of this meeting is a court record, taken down by imperial notaries. In the summer of 411 the emperor ordered our whole quarrel settled at law. He sent Flavius Marcellinus, a tribune and notary, to Carthage to judge it. Our bishops came, and the roll of their mandates was read out name by name.

Marcellinus offered our bishops chairs, because it weighed on him to sit while so many venerable men stood. Petilian thanked him and refused. Christ himself had stood before his governor, he said, so how could we refuse to stand? Our bishops stood for three days.

Emeritus of Caesarea carried our argument, and he held the court to its procedure before its substance. The other side claimed the name Catholic, and Petilian answered that the name meant nothing until the case was decided. Marcellinus agreed that the name belonged to whichever side the truth was found with. Then he said he was bound by the emperor's written order, which had already given them that name.

On the third day the argument reached Scripture, and Augustine argued from the wheat and the weeds that the church holds good and bad together. Emeritus answered him verse for verse from the same books. He signed the record of his words again and again with his appeal reserved. The verdict is not in what we have, because the acts break off before any sentence is given.
documented_stories.title: Three Days Standing Before a Judge Already Told Who Was Right

floor_note.text: This world confessed the same faith the councils of its own century put into words: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God, and Christ truly God and truly human. In the vast literature written to destroy it, it is called schismatic on nearly every page and heretic on none - because no charge of heresy could be made to stick in either direction. What was disputed was never the creed. It was a narrower and sharper question: whether a bishop's own conduct under persecution could void what his ordaining hand later gave to everyone who received it.

highlights.note: Latin for those who handed over. It names clergy accused of giving the scriptures to the persecutors. This church held that such a man could no longer baptize or ordain.
The senior bishop of a church. This church's primate sat at Carthage, and its rival claimed the same seat for its own man.
A Roman official who judged court cases in a province. One cleared Felix of the charge. Another put Isaac and Maximianus on trial.
A written ruling from an emperor. In 411 the judge held that an earlier rescript had already given the name Catholic to the rival church.
The word means universal. Both churches claimed it as their title. The state granted it to the rival, and this church called that side Caecilianists.
The shared faith in the Trinity and in Christ held across Latin North Africa. Both churches confessed it. They split over which bishops were valid.
People who followed Maximian, a deacon made rival head of the church in 393. A larger meeting of bishops at Bagai condemned them in 394.

highlights.label: Diocletian's persecution
highlights.note: Diocletian and the emperors who ruled with him hunted Christians in these years. They ordered clergy to hand over the scriptures and church vessels to be destroyed.
The Vandals invaded Roman North Africa in 429 and took Carthage in 439. That ended the Roman state that this church had defined itself against.
A hearing at Rome in 313, where Constantine sent the dispute after this church petitioned him. It ruled against this church, which rejected the result.
A meeting of bishops in 314. Constantine sent the African dispute there. It ruled against this church, and this church rejected the ruling.
A court hearing in 411, ordered by the emperor to settle the quarrel. The judge Marcellinus ran it. The record stops before any verdict.
Primate at Carthage from about 313 until his death in exile about 347. The movement is named for him. Not one page of his own survives.
Bishop of Constantina for this church. With Emeritus, he spoke for it in 411. His letters survive only because Augustine quoted them to answer them.
A writer in this church in the 370s and 380s who composed the Book of Rules, seven rules for reading scripture. A council reportedly condemned him around 380.
Catholic bishop of Hippo from 395 or 396 until 430. He wrote against this church and argued against it at the 411 Conference.
A Catholic bishop of Milevis who wrote seven books against this church in the 360s and revised them about 385. Most of its early history reaches us through him.
The imperial officer sent to judge the hearing of 411. He belonged to neither church. He was put to death in 413 on another charge.

highlights.label: Paul and Macarius
highlights.note: Paul and Macarius, who forced this church to join its rival in 347 and 348. Their force sometimes killed.
A Roman province of North Africa and the heartland of this church. Its towns in these stories, such as Cirta and Bagai, lie in today's Algeria.
An ancient city of Numidia, now the city of Constantine in Algeria. Bishops met there in a council whose date is disputed, 305, 307 or later.
Town of the bishop Felix, who consecrated Caecilian. Its ruins, at Henchir es Souar, lie in today's Tunisia.
A town in Numidia where 310 bishops met in 394. Its ruins, at Ksar Baghai, lie in today's Algeria.
A town in the Roman province of Byzacena, where Maximian was made rival head of the church in 393. Its exact site is unknown.
The cliff where Marculus was held and killed. It is probably the site now called Henchir Encedda, in today's Algeria.
The place in Numidia where Marculus was seized. It is identified with Ksar el Kelb, in today's Algeria.

highlights.label: Constantine
highlights.note: Constantine, who became emperor in 306. He had the charge against Felix tried, and the trial ended in 314 or 315.
A bishop of this church who used soldiers to bring the two condemned bishops back. He is a different man from Optatus of Milevis.
The chief city of Roman Africa, where both rival churches had their bishop. Its ruins lie in today's Tunis, in Tunisia.

legacy.text: One thread carried past this world's own horizon in a way its own founders could hardly have predicted. The Book of Rules, the one substantial work of biblical interpretation this world produced, survived the council that condemned its own author. It crossed over to the side that had defeated this communion and shaped how Augustine, and generations of readers after him, learned to read Scripture - a transmission this world's own record does not explain and does not claim to.

The two-party contest itself did not end when this world's own window closes in 439. It continued under Vandal and then Byzantine rule for roughly a further century and a half, still legislated against, until Pope Gregory the Great wrote letters in the 590s pressing for an inquiry into Donatist rebaptism still being practiced in Numidia. After that, this world's own record simply falls silent. No line from it to any communion a person could visit today is documented anywhere, and this world's own Living Tradition Status has never been confirmed.

read_first.note: The earliest sustained narrative of this world's own founding decade, written roughly five decades after the events by the Catholic bishop this communion regarded as its opponent - and the source through which most of what survives of that founding decade actually reaches us.

source.citation: Optatus of Milevis, Against the Donatists (De schismate Donatistarum), trans. O.R. Vassall-Phillips (London: Longmans, Green & Co., 1917)

read_first.note: Three books quoting a Donatist bishop's own letters clause by clause in order to refute them - the fullest surviving Donatist voice, reaching us because it was chosen for answerability, not because anyone wanted it preserved for its own sake.

source.citation: Augustine of Hippo, Answer to the Letters of Petilian, the Donatist (Contra litteras Petiliani), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, vol. IV

read_first.note: The transcript of the 411 Conference of Carthage - the one place in this world's record where its own bishops argue their own case, in their own recorded words, with no adversary curating what survived. Also this corpus's worst-damaged scan, so exact wording throughout is a careful reading of a difficult copy, not a settled critical edition.

source.citation: J.-P. Migne (ed.), Patrologiae Cursus Completus, Series Latina, Tomus XI (Paris)

relations_summary.text: This world's own refusal to grant the state any standing to judge the church is the mirror image of a neighboring world's own opposite condition: Imperial and Juridical Christianity, where church office became a form of state-adjacent power from Constantine's own reign onward, and where the same Constantine this world petitioned once and then refused for a century is that other world's own initiating figure. And this world's once-for-all rebaptism is the opposite answer Cappadocian Christianity gave to the identical question - how someone from the other side comes back in - which trained its own people to hold graded penance and graded reception as instruments of exactness rather than as a wall. Neither comparison is a claim that either world resolves the other; both are genuine divergences this world's own records name directly, not thematic echoes assumed from outside.

sourcing.text: This world's evidence survives in inverse proportion to how directly it can be checked without a hostile hand mediating it. Nearly the whole textual record passed through two Catholic writers, Optatus of Milevis and Augustine of Hippo, before reaching us - and that concentration is named as this world's own central evidentiary problem, not a background caveat. Four short texts speak as this communion rather than about it, plus the transcript of the 411 Conference, where for once no adversary chose which words to keep. The clearest exception of all was never a text to begin with: two words, Deo laudes, cut into stone. What this world's own record cannot supply at all is any specific report, excavation, or plan of the rooms these words were spoken in - Numidian basilica archaeology remains honestly undone in this world's own source ecology, so this world knows its own shout far better than the room it was shouted in. And one further live scholarly contest runs through the whole record rather than sitting in one place: whether the hostile portrait of this world's rural members, the Circumcellions, reflects their real character or mainly their opponents' polemic. That question is not adjudicated here.

story.text: From around 311 until 439, two rival churches stood side by side in Roman North Africa, centered on Carthage. Both confessed the same Nicene faith, word for word. They split over one question. Could a bishop's conduct under persecution void what his hand later gave? One side said yes. It called itself the Church of the Martyrs, the one pure, persecuted and true church. History calls its members Donatists, after an early bishop, though nothing suggests they chose that name.

The quarrel began in the persecution of 303 to 305. Officials demanded that clergy hand over the scriptures or die. Some did. Others refused and suffered for it. This church held that what a minister did in that moment decided whether his hand could be trusted afterward. When it ended, Caecilian was elected bishop of Carthage. Felix of Aptungi, who ordained him, was accused of handing over the scriptures. If that was true, this church held, the new bishop was no bishop at all. A rival party made Majorinus bishop in his place. The emperor later had the charge against Felix tried, and Felix was cleared. This church never accepted that one hearing could settle the whole dispute.

The doctrine had one public consequence, repeated for a century. Anyone who crossed over from the rival church was washed again. This church never called it a second baptism. A hand from a broken line had given nothing the first time, so its font marked a person's first true entry into the church. Imperial edicts named the practice as an offense.

Persecution came a second time in 347 and 348, and this time it came at the rival church's urging, through the emperor's commissioners. It gave this church the martyrs it remembered. Bishop Marculus, after four days of fasting, was shown a cup, a crown and a palm, then thrown from a cliff called Novapetra. Two laymen of Carthage, Isaac and Maximianus, were flogged and sunk in the sea. Every year, at the grave, the church read such accounts aloud again.

By the later fourth century this was a full parallel church. It had its own bishops, basilicas and councils, and it contested the same towns as its rival. In Numidia it was simply the ordinary church of the countryside.

Its bishop Donatus is remembered for one line, kept by the man who wrote against him. What has the emperor to do with the church? Rome's hearing in 313 and the Council of Arles in 314 ruled against this church, and it rejected both rulings. A court run on a state's terms, in its view, was not the church judging itself. Still, its own texts admit exceptions. Three times it turned to the state when that served its case. It petitioned Constantine in 313 and Julian in 361. In the 390s it invoked imperial law against its own breakaway Maximianists.

At the Conference of Carthage in 411, two hundred and seventy-nine of its bishops faced two hundred and eighty-six from the other side. They stood before an imperial judge, as Christ had stood before his governor, and refused the chairs he offered. The judge granted that the name Catholic belonged to whichever side held the truth. Then he ruled that an imperial rescript had already given the name to the other side.

The record closes in 439, when a Vandal army took Carthage. That ended the Roman rule this church had defined itself against. The contest went on under the Vandals, and then under the Eastern empire. In the 590s Pope Gregory the Great wrote letters about rebaptism still going on in Numidia, and pressed for an inquiry. After that, the record goes silent. No line from it to any church alive today has ever been shown.

Almost everything known about this church was written by two men arguing against it. Its own voice survives in four short texts, and in two words cut into pillars near Bagai: Deo laudes, praise to God. No hostile hand stands between those words and a modern reader.

dates.display: primate of this communion from c. 313, succeeding Majorinus, until c. 347; exiled after the Macarian repression and dead in exile. Birth date unknown; the byname Magnus is the tradition's, not a title he is recorded claiming.

names.name: Donatus, our bishop at Carthage
Donatus the Great, Donatist bishop of Carthage (primate c. 313 - c. 347)

voices.hedge: Almost everything said of Donatus reaches this record through a hostile source arguing against him. The proposal that he personally preached the annual commemorative sermon read every twelfth of March is a modern scholarly hypothesis, floated and then hedged by the man who made it - never an attested fact, and not adopted here.
voices.text: Donatus succeeded Majorinus as bishop of Carthage around 313 and led this communion for more than three decades - long enough that history remembers the whole movement by his name, though nothing suggests his own people chose that name for themselves. He left no writing of his own. His single most quoted line survives only because the bishop who opposed him recorded it in order to answer it: what has the emperor to do with the church? He was exiled after the Macarian repression of 347-348 and died in exile.

dates.display: bishop of Constantina, the renamed Cirta, from the 390s; author of the letters Augustine answered in three books around 400-403; one of the seven Donatist pleaders at the 411 Conference of Carthage and, with Emeritus, one of the two principal voices there

names.name: Petilian, our bishop at Constantina
Petilian of Constantina (Cirta), Donatist bishop (fl. c. 395-411 and after)

voices.hedge: Petilian's letters are visible only in the clauses Augustine chose to quote in order to answer them - a preservation mechanism that selects for what is answerable, not for completeness. The 411 transcript is a real exception, since nobody there was choosing his words for him, but the surviving scan of it carries the worst OCR damage in this world's whole corpus, so even his recorded speech there is a careful reading of a difficult copy, not a certified text.
voices.text: Petilian became bishop of Constantina, the renamed Cirta, in the 390s and was, by volume, this world's fullest surviving voice - because Augustine quoted his letters clause by clause across three books in order to refute them. At the great Conference of Carthage in 411 he argued in a different register entirely: on an open transcript, thanking the judge for the offer of a chair and refusing it, because Christ himself had not refused to stand before his own governor.

dates.display: born about 350 at Caesarea in Mauretania Caesariensis; trained in rhetoric and the liberal arts; drafted the sentence of the Council of Bagai in 394, which implies established authority by that date; at the height of his reputation at the 411 Conference; older and embittered at a further dialogue with Augustine at Caesarea itself in 418

names.name: Emeritus, our bishop at Caesarea
Emeritus of Caesarea in Mauretania (b. c. 350 at Caesarea, modern Cherchel; fl. 394-418)

voices.hedge: Even this best-attested voice has real limits. The transcript survives in this corpus's single worst-damaged scan. Only roughly nineteen hundred of its 144,733 lines have been read so far. That was a systematic search on Emeritus's own name, not the whole document. His later dialogue with Augustine in 418 is a separate work. This world does not draw on it at all.
voices.text: Emeritus, bishop of Caesarea in Mauretania, carried this communion's case for three days at the Conference of Carthage in 411, on the best evidentiary footing any figure in this world's record holds: his own words, taken down by an imperial notary as he spoke them. He held the court to its own procedure before its substance, and when the argument finally reached Scripture, answered a reading of the wheat and the tares verse for verse, out of the same books. He signed the transcript of his own words again and again with the same qualified formula: his appeal reserved.

dates.display: seized at Vegesela in Numidia during the Macarian repression and killed at a cliff called Novapetra; the Passio's own heading dates the commemoration to a day in late November without giving a year, and the 347-348 dating comes from the standard field literature

names.name: Marculus, blessed martyr
Marculus (d. c. 347/348, during the Macarian repression; subject of the Passio Marculi)

voices.hedge: The bare fact of his death is corroborated even by hostile witnesses, though for two different and incompatible reasons: one argues the killing was deserved punishment for schism, the other disputes whether the word martyr even applies. The vision, the unbroken fall, and the light over the place afterward are this world's own testimony about what his death meant, not independently verified events, and they are not presented here as more.
voices.text: This world remembers Marculus as a man who had already given up worldly advancement before the persecution that killed him ever found him. Seized during the Macarian repression, he was flogged, paraded through several Numidian towns, and held four days at a cliff called Novapetra, where he was shown, in the fast, a vision of a cup, a crown, and a palm. He was thrown from the cliff before dawn.

dates.display: active as a writer and preacher within this communion in the 370s and 380s; rebuked by Parmenian and, it is reported, condemned by a council around 380; the Liber Regularum written in the same period and never suppressed

names.name: Tyconius
Tyconius (fl. c. 370-390; author of the Liber Regularum; condemned c. 380)

voices.hedge: His own seven Rules for reading Scripture survive complete among this world's own sources - but they have not been read in depth here, and everything said of their content here runs through a 1920 secondary chapter rather than through Tyconius's own Latin. The mechanism of his condemnation carries Augustine's own reporting hedge, 'it is reported,' which is kept here rather than smoothed into settled fact. His own formal standing inside this communion, before or after the rupture, is deliberately left open by this world's own construction record.
voices.text: Tyconius was the one systematic theologian this world produced, and the one it silenced. A layman, he argued from Scripture that the church was spread across the whole earth - an argument built well enough that his own bishop at Carthage told him never to preach it again. He did not recant, and did not defect to the other side either; he kept saying it from inside the party that had told him to stop, and was cut off for good.

tile.text: Between 311 and 439, in Roman North Africa, two churches stood in nearly every town, each with its own bishop, altar, and unbroken line of ordination. The rift began with an accusation: that the man who consecrated the new bishop of Carthage had once handed the scriptures over to be burned. If that hand was tainted, this world held, everything it touched afterward was empty too - so a whole rival church grew up around one demand: wash again, by a hand that has never broken. This communion called itself the Church of the Martyrs. When persecution came a second time, at a rival Christian party's own urging, it kept the names of its dead and read their story aloud every year at the grave. It refused any emperor's standing to decide who the true church was - though three times, when it served the case, it turned to that same emperor's courts anyway, and said so plainly in the same breath as the refusal. Nearly everything known of this world comes from the two bishops who wrote against it. Four short texts, and two words cut into stone, are what survive in its own voice.
